short: The total value of everything in your account right now.
detail: It adds up what your funds are worth today and any cash you have. It changes on days the market is open.
example: If your funds are worth $900 and you have $100 in cash, your balance is $1,000.

short: Money you move from your bank into your investing account.
detail: A deposit lands as cash first. If auto-invest is on, it then buys your chosen mix for you.
example: Rosa moves $150 from her bank on the first of each month.

short: A deposit that happens on its own on the same day each month.
detail: You set it up once. After that, the money moves each month without you doing anything. You can stop it at any time.
example: A $150 deposit on the first of every month.

short: A setting that puts each deposit into your chosen mix for you.
detail: When it is on, new money buys your funds on the day it arrives. When it is paused, new money waits as cash until you decide. You can turn it on or off at any time.
example: With auto-invest on, a $150 deposit buys your funds on the same day.

short: A deposit your bank sent back instead of paying it.
detail: Banks do this for a few reasons, such as the account being low that day. The money never reached your investing account, so nothing you own was sold or lost.
example: You ask for a $150 deposit on the 1st, and it comes back on the 3rd.

short: Money in your account that is not in a fund yet.
detail: Cash does not go down when the market drops. It also does not grow when the market goes up.
example: A new deposit waits as cash until it is used to buy a fund.

short: A basket that holds many investments at once.
detail: When you buy a share of a fund, you own a tiny piece of everything in the basket. This is an easy way to own a lot of companies with a little money.
example: One fund might hold small pieces of 3,000 companies.

short: A fund that copies a set list of companies instead of picking them by hand.
detail: Nobody has to choose which companies to buy, so the yearly fee is often low. The fund goes up and down with the whole list.
example: A fund that owns every company on a list of the biggest ones.

short: A short nickname for a fund, a bit like a username.
detail: Real tickers are a few letters long. In this demo, every ticker starts with FL- so you always know it is made up.
example: FL-BROAD is the ticker for the Broad U.S. Market Index Fund in this demo.

short: One unit of a fund that you can buy or sell.
detail: Each share has a price. When the price goes up, every share you own is worth more.
example: If one share costs $50 and you own 2 shares, you have $100.

short: A piece of one share, so you can invest a small amount.
detail: You do not need to buy a whole share. If a share costs $100, you can still invest $10 and own one tenth of a share.
example: $10 buys 0.1 of a $100 share.

short: What one share costs at the latest price.
detail: The price changes on each day the market is open. On weekends and holidays, you see the last price from when the market was open.
example: A share might cost $95 on Monday and $97 on Friday.

short: What your shares are worth at the latest price.
detail: It is the number of shares you own times the latest price. It moves each day the market is open.
example: 3 shares at $20 each have a value of $60.

short: The total of your deposits that went through.
detail: It does not count deposits that were sent back. Compare it with your balance to see how much the market added or took away.
example: You put in $500, then $150 five times. That adds up to $1,250.

short: The total amount you spent to buy a fund.
detail: Compare it with the fund's value today. If the value is higher, you are up. If it is lower, you are down.
example: You spent $60 on a fund that is now worth $66. You are up $6.

short: How much more or less your money is worth than what you put in.
detail: Being up means it grew. Being down means it shrank. Until you sell, it can still change.
example: You put in $100 and it is worth $105. You are up $5.

short: How much your money grew or shrank, shown as a percent.
detail: A percent makes it easy to compare big and small amounts. A 5% return on $100 is $5. A 5% return on $1,000 is $50.
example: Up $5 on $100 is a 5% return.

short: A small payment some funds make to the people who own them.
detail: Stock funds pass on part of what companies earn. Bond funds pass on the interest from their loans. In First Leaf, the payment lands in your cash.
example: A bond fund pays you 50 cents on the 15th of the month.

short: What a fund charges each year to run, shown as a percent.
detail: A 0.10% fee costs about $1 a year for every $1,000 you have in the fund. The fee comes out of the fund's value, so you never get a bill. That is why it is easy to miss.
example: With $1,000 in a fund, a 0.04% fee is 40 cents a year. A 0.75% fee is $7.50 a year.

short: Small pieces of companies that you can own.
detail: Stocks can grow a lot over many years. They can also drop fast. That is why they have more ups and downs.
example: A stock fund owns small pieces of many companies.

short: Loans you make to a government or a company.
detail: They pay you back over time with a little extra. Bonds usually move up and down less than stocks, but they also tend to grow less.
example: A bond fund owns thousands of small loans.

short: How your money is split between kinds of funds, like stocks and bonds.
detail: More stocks means more ups and downs. More bonds means a calmer ride. You pick the split that feels right for you.
example: A mix of 85% stocks and 15% bonds.

short: Owning many different things so one bad one hurts you less.
detail: If one company has a bad year, the others can help balance it out. Funds do a lot of this for you.
example: Owning 3,000 companies instead of just one.

short: Moving money around so your mix goes back to the split you picked.
detail: Some funds grow faster than others, so your mix slowly drifts. Rebalancing puts it back. Some people do it once or twice a year.
example: You picked 85% stocks, but now you have 90%. Rebalancing brings it back to 85%.

short: How much a fund's price tends to jump around.
detail: We rate each fund from 1, calm, to 5, bumpy. Bumpy funds can grow more over time, but they can also fall more on a bad day.
example: The Calm Reserve Fund is a 1. The Clean Energy Theme Fund is a 5.

short: When your money earns money, and then that new money earns money too.
detail: It starts small and speeds up over time, like a snowball rolling downhill. The more years it has, the bigger it gets.
example: $100 that grows 6% becomes $106. The next year, the 6% is on $106, not $100.

short: The short wait after you buy or sell before the trade is final.
detail: In the U.S., most trades are final one business day later. Until then, the trade shows as settling.
example: You buy on Monday. It is final on Tuesday.

source.label: Investor.gov: New T+1 settlement cycle (U.S. SEC)

short: Whether your deposits are keeping up with your plan.
detail: It only looks at the money you put in. It does not change when the market goes up or down.
example: You planned to put in $1,400 by now and put in $1,250. You are $150 behind.

short: Pretend money for trying things before you do them for real.
detail: You start with $1,000 that is not real. Nothing you do here touches your real account, and you can start over at any time.
example: Buy a fund with pretend money and see how it would have moved.

short: All the people buying and selling investments.
detail: When more people want to buy, prices go up. When more people want to sell, prices go down. It is open on weekdays, but not on some holidays.
example: Prices can change every minute while the market is open.

short: Every fund, price and person in First Leaf is made up.
detail: First Leaf was built for a design case study. Nothing here is real money, and nothing here tells you what to buy or sell.
example: Rosa is not a real person, and FL-BROAD is not a real fund.
